title: Lieb und Leid theilen
source: Brüder Grimm, Kinder- und Hausmärchen, Band 2, 7. Auflage (Ausgabe letzter Hand), Dieterich, Göttingen 1857, KHM 170. Text from Wikisource („Lieb und Leid theilen (1857)“, twice proofread against the original). Fresh translation made directly from the German; 1857 spelling preserved exactly.
about: A tailor who beats his wife is made to promise the court that from now on he will “Lieb und Leid theilen” with her — share joy and sorrow, a set phrase from the old marriage vow meaning to stand by a spouse for better and worse. He keeps the letter of it by a piece of cruel wordplay: when he hits her it pleases him and pains her, so joy and sorrow are, he claims, shared after all. The judges are not fooled.

sentences.t: Es war einmal ein Schneider, der war ein zänkischer Mensch, und seine Frau, die gut, fleißig und fromm war, konnte es ihm niemals recht machen.
sentences.l: There was once a tailor, he was a quarrelsome man, and his wife, who was good, hard-working and pious, could never make it right for him.
sentences.i: There was once a tailor who was a quarrelsome man, and his wife, who was good, hard-working and pious, could never satisfy him.
sentences.n: der war — the relative pronoun der stands here almost as a demonstrative, “that one was”, an old-fashioned way of hanging a second clause on a noun. es jemandem recht machen is to satisfy someone, to do a thing to his liking; the German says only “make it right for him”.

sentences.t: Was sie that, er war unzufrieden, brummte, schalt, raufte und schlug sie.
sentences.l: Whatever she did, he was dissatisfied, growled, scolded, tore at her and beat her.
sentences.i: Whatever she did, he was dissatisfied — he growled, scolded, tore at her and beat her.
sentences.n: that is the 1857 spelling of tat, from thun, modern tun. raufen here is transitive and violent: to tear or pull at somebody, usually by the hair. The tale states the beating flatly in its second sentence and never once softens it.

sentences.t: Als die Obrigkeit endlich davon hörte, ließ sie ihn vorfordern und ins Gefängnis setzen, damit er sich bessern sollte.
sentences.l: When the authorities at last heard of it, they had him summoned and put into prison, so that he should mend himself.
sentences.i: When the magistrates at last heard of it, they had him summoned and put in prison, so that he should mend his ways.
sentences.n: die Obrigkeit, the local magistracy, is singular in German — sie ließ, it had — where English wants a plural. lassen with an infinitive is causative: had him summoned, had him set in prison. sich bessern is to reform, to mend one’s ways.

sentences.t: Er saß eine Zeitlang bei Wasser und Brot, dann wurde er wieder freigelassen, mußte aber geloben seine Frau nicht mehr zu schlagen, sondern friedlich mit ihr zu leben, Lieb und Leid zu theilen, wie sichs unter Eheleuten gebührt.
sentences.l: He sat a while on water and bread, then he was set free again, but had to vow not to beat his wife any more, but to live peaceably with her, to share love and sorrow, as is fitting between married people.
sentences.i: He sat a while on bread and water; then he was let out again, but he had to vow that he would beat his wife no more, and would live peaceably with her, and share love and sorrow, as is fitting between married people.
sentences.n: Lieb und Leid theilen — to share love and sorrow — was the standing formula of the German marriage vow, the promise to hold to one another in good times and bad. The court is quoting the wedding rather than inventing a sentence, and everything that follows turns on the tailor taking the formula at its word. bei Wasser und Brot sitzen is the ordinary phrase for prison fare; wie sichs gebührt, as is fitting.

sentences.t: Eine Zeitlang gieng es gut, dann aber gerieth er wieder in seine alte Weise, war mürrisch und zänkisch.
sentences.l: For a while it went well, but then he fell back into his old way, was surly and quarrelsome.
sentences.i: For a while it went well, but then he fell back into his old ways, and was surly and quarrelsome.
sentences.n: gerieth is the 1857 spelling of geriet, from gerathen, modern geraten — in etwas gerathen is to fall or drift into something, not to choose it.

sentences.t: Und weil er sie nicht schlagen durfte, wollte er sie bei den Haaren packen und raufen.
sentences.l: And because he was not allowed to beat her, he wanted to seize her by the hair and tear at it.
sentences.i: And because he was not permitted to beat her, he took to seizing her by the hair and tearing at it.
sentences.n: dürfen is to be allowed to, not to be able to: the prohibition is the court’s, and the tailor is working round it rather than obeying it.

sentences.t: Die Frau entwischte ihm und sprang auf den Hof hinaus, er lief aber mit der Elle und Scheere hinter ihr her, jagte sie herum und warf ihr die Elle und Scheere, und was ihm sonst zur Hand war, nach.
sentences.l: The wife slipped away from him and sprang out into the yard, but he ran after her with the yardstick and the shears, chased her about and threw the yardstick and shears after her, and whatever else was to his hand.
sentences.i: The wife slipped away from him and sprang out into the yard, but he ran after her with his yardstick and shears, chased her round and threw the yardstick and the shears after her, and whatever else came to his hand.
sentences.n: hinter ihr her laufen is to run along behind somebody. warf … nach is nachwerfen, to throw after, and its particle waits to the very end of the sentence, past a whole inserted clause — a long separation even by German standards. Elle and Scheere are the tailor’s own tools: his trade is what he throws.

sentences.t: Wenn er sie traf, so lachte er, und wenn er sie fehlte, so tobte und wetterte er.
sentences.l: When he hit her, he laughed, and when he missed her, he raged and stormed.
sentences.n: treffen and fehlen make a pair here — to hit and to miss, of a thrown thing — and the pair comes back at the end of the tale as the tailor’s defence. wettern is literally to make weather, to thunder.

sentences.t: Er trieb es so lange bis die Nachbaren der Frau zu Hilfe kamen.
sentences.l: He carried on so long until the neighbours came to the wife’s help.
sentences.i: He kept it up until the neighbours came to the wife’s help.
sentences.n: es treiben is to carry on, to keep at something. Nachbaren is the older plural of Nachbar; modern German has Nachbarn.

sentences.t: Der Schneider ward wieder vor die Obrigkeit gerufen und an sein Versprechen erinnert.
sentences.l: The tailor was called again before the authorities and reminded of his promise.
sentences.n: ward is the old simple past of werden, and here builds the passive: was called, was reminded. erinnern takes an — an sein Versprechen erinnert, reminded of his promise.

sentences.t: „Liebe Herrn,“ antwortete er, „ich habe gehalten was ich gelobt habe, ich habe sie nicht geschlagen, sondern Lieb und Leid mit ihr getheilt.“
sentences.l: “Dear sirs,” he answered, “I have kept what I vowed, I have not beaten her, but shared love and sorrow with her.”
sentences.i: “Good sirs,” he answered, “I have kept what I vowed: I have not beaten her, but shared love and sorrow with her.”
sentences.n: gelobt is from geloben, to vow, not from loben, to praise — the participles look alike, and the tailor’s whole defence rests on the difference. He is quoting the court’s own words back at it.

sentences.t: „Wie kann das sein,“ sprach der Richter, „da sie abermals so große Klage über Euch führt?“
sentences.l: “How can that be,” said the judge, “when she brings so great a complaint against you once more?”
sentences.i: “How can that be,” said the judge, “when she brings so heavy a complaint against you yet again?”
sentences.n: Klage führen über is the legal phrase, to lodge a complaint against. Euch is the older respectful address a court would use to a man, and it is still simply “you”. abermals is once again.

sentences.t: „Ich habe sie nicht geschlagen, sondern ihr nur, weil sie so wunderlich aussah, die Haare mit der Hand kämmen wollen: sie ist mir aber entwichen und hat mich böslich verlassen.
sentences.l: “I have not beaten her, but only wanted, because she looked so strange, to comb her hair with my hand: but she got away from me and wickedly abandoned me.
sentences.i: “I have not beaten her; I only wanted to comb her hair with my hand, because she looked so wild — but she got away from me and wickedly abandoned me.
sentences.n: The tailor has begun to talk like a court document: entweichen, to abscond, and böslich verlassen, wilfully to desert, are both terms out of matrimonial law, so that running away from him becomes an offence she has committed. habe … kämmen wollen is the double infinitive German uses in the perfect of a modal: I have wanted to comb.

sentences.t: Da bin ich ihr nachgeeilt und habe, damit sie zu ihrer Pflicht zurückkehre, als eine gutgemeinte Erinnerung nachgeworfen was mir eben zur Hand war.
sentences.l: Then I hurried after her and, so that she should return to her duty, threw after her, as a well-meant reminder, whatever was just then to my hand.
sentences.i: So I hurried after her, and, so that she should return to her duty, threw after her — as a well-meant reminder — whatever came to my hand.
sentences.n: zurückkehre is a subjunctive of purpose: so that she should return. Erinnerung here is a reminder, not a memory. gutgemeint, well-meant, is the tailor’s own word for the flying shears, and the 1857 text lets it stand without comment.

sentences.t: Ich habe auch Lieb und Leid mit ihr getheilt, denn so oft ich sie getroffen habe, ist es mir lieb gewesen und ihr leid: habe ich sie aber gefehlt, so ist es ihr lieb gewesen, mir aber leid.“
sentences.l: I have also shared love and sorrow with her, for as often as I have hit her it has been a joy to me and a sorrow to her: but if I missed her, then it was a joy to her and a sorrow to me.”
sentences.i: I have shared love and sorrow with her too, for every time I hit her it was a joy to me and a sorrow to her; and when I missed her, it was a joy to her and a sorrow to me.”
sentences.n: Here the tale does its work in one sentence: lieb and leid are the plain adjectives, dear and grievous — es ist mir lieb, it is a pleasure to me — so the marriage formula Lieb und Leid theilen falls apart into its two separate words and is met to the letter. Whether the German is laughing at the tailor or at a court that handed him such a sentence, it does not say.

sentences.t: Die Richter waren aber mit dieser Antwort nicht zufrieden, sondern ließen ihm seinen verdienten Lohn auszahlen.
sentences.l: The judges, however, were not satisfied with this answer, but had his deserved wages paid out to him.
sentences.i: But the judges were not satisfied with this answer, and had him paid the wages he had earned.
sentences.n: seinen verdienten Lohn auszahlen is grimly literal: Lohn is wages, and paying a man the wages he has earned is the ordinary German way of saying he got what was coming to him — here a beating in his turn. The tale ends on the phrase and explains nothing further.

glossary.bessern: bessern — to reform, to mend (infinitive; sich bessern, to mend one’s ways); not besser, better
glossary.es: es — it; also the impersonal object of a fixed phrase (‘es ihm recht machen’ = to satisfy him; ‘er trieb es’ = he carried on)
glossary.führt: führen — leads, carries on (3rd sg. present; ‘Klage führen über’ = to lodge a complaint against)
glossary.gefehlt: fehlen — missed (a target) (past participle; ‘habe ich sie gefehlt’ = if I missed her)
glossary.gelobt: geloben — vowed, pledged (past participle, gelobt; not loben, to praise — the tailor’s defence turns on the difference)
glossary.leid: das Leid — sorrow, grief (‘Lieb und Leid theilen’); also the predicative adjective leid, grievous: ‘es ist mir leid’ = it grieves me
glossary.lieb: lieb — dear, pleasing (‘es ist mir lieb’ = it is a pleasure to me); in ‘Lieb und Leid’ it stands as a noun, love
glossary.ließen: lassen — had (something) done (3rd pl. past, causative: ‘ließen … auszahlen’ = had it paid out)
glossary.raufen: raufen — to pull, to tear at (the hair) (infinitive; jemanden bei den Haaren raufen)
glossary.traf: treffen — hit, struck (3rd sg. past; of a thrown thing: ‘wenn er sie traf’ = when he hit her); elsewhere to meet
